text: Johnson does not found his judgment upon his own admiration, since the admiration of a single critic may be no more than the taste of one age and the bent of one temper. He asks instead what time has done to the work. The writer whose reputation rests on the fashion of his day, on the customs of a place or the quarrels of a party, may be praised while that fashion lasts; but fashions pass, and the praise that leaned upon them passes too. Those works alone have proved their worth which continue to please readers who share none of the circumstances of the first audience, for such readers come to the trial without partiality. They have no friendship with the author and no stake in his opinions; they read him only because he still gives them pleasure.
